title: Circuit components — diodes, LDRs and thermistors
examTip: I-V graphs are favourite exam targets. Know the shape for a fixed resistor, a diode and a filament bulb. Be ready to explain each shape in terms of resistance.
introTips: Before you read, sketch the I-V graph for a fixed resistor and for a diode. Then check if you were right.
Make flashcards for the LDR and thermistor. What happens to resistance when the physical quantity increases?
Circuit symbols come up in every paper. Practise drawing them from memory.
intro: Why does your phone charger get warm but barely flicker the lights? Why do street lamps switch on by themselves at dusk? The answer is how different components respond to the conditions around them. Some change their resistance with light. Some change it with heat. Some only let current through in one direction. These components are the base of every electronic device you have ever used.

keyPoints.heading: Fixed resistors and variable resistors
keyPoints.content: A fixed resistor has a constant resistance, whatever the temperature, light or other conditions. It follows Ohm's Law: V = IR. Here V is voltage (volts, V), I is current (amps, A) and R is resistance (ohms, Ω). A variable resistor (also called a rheostat) lets you change the resistance by hand. You slide a contact along a resistive wire or track. They are used in dimmer switches, volume controls and lab experiments to control current. Take an I-V graph for an ohmic conductor (a fixed resistor at constant temperature). You get a straight line through the origin. Current is directly proportional to voltage. The steeper the line, the lower the resistance. Doubling the resistance halves the gradient. Worked example: R = 10 Ω, V = 5 V → I = V ÷ R = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 A.
writeBullets: Fixed resistor — resistance stays the same at all voltages and temperatures
Variable resistor (rheostat) — the user can change the resistance by hand
Ohm's Law — V = IR. Current is proportional to voltage for ohmic conductors
I-V graph: straight line through the origin. Constant gradient = constant resistance
Steeper gradient on I-V graph → lower resistance (more current per volt)
Units: V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms

keyTerms.def: A component whose resistance stays constant as voltage changes — produces a straight-line I-V graph through the origin.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed manually, used to control current in a circuit.
The opposition to current flow; measured in ohms (Ω). R = V ÷ I.

keyPoints.memTip: Straight line = straight behaviour = fixed resistor. If the graph curves, something is changing.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up gradient and resistance. A steeper gradient means MORE current for the same voltage. So it means LOWER resistance.

keyPoints.heading: Diodes
keyPoints.content: A diode is a component that only lets current flow in one direction, the forward direction. In reverse bias (the wrong direction), resistance is extremely high and almost no current flows. On an I-V graph, the diode shows a flat line near zero for negative voltages. Then there is a sudden steep rise once the forward threshold voltage is passed. This is ~0.7 V for silicon diodes. The circuit symbol is a triangle pointing the way conventional current flows. A vertical bar blocks flow the other way. An LED (light-emitting diode) is a diode that gives out light when current flows forwards. It also has a threshold voltage. It gives out photons as electrons lose energy crossing the junction. LEDs are used in TVs, phone screens, traffic lights and energy-efficient lighting. Diodes are used in rectification. This means turning alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC), for example in phone chargers.
writeBullets: Diode — lets current flow forwards only. Reverse bias gives near-zero current
Forward threshold voltage — ~0.7 V for silicon. The diode won't conduct below this
I-V graph — flat for negative V, then a sudden steep rise above the threshold voltage
LED — gives out light when forward current flows. Used in energy-efficient lighting
Rectification — using diodes to convert AC → DC in power supplies
Circuit symbol — triangle + bar. The triangle points the way conventional current flows

keyTerms.def: A component that allows current to flow in one direction only, with very high resistance in reverse bias.
Light-emitting diode — a diode that releases light energy when current flows through it in the forward direction.
The minimum voltage needed for a diode to conduct; approximately 0.7 V for silicon diodes.
Converting AC to DC using one or more diodes, as in phone chargers and power adapters.

keyPoints.memTip: The triangle in the symbol points the way current can go. It is like an arrow saying 'this way only'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The flat part of the diode I-V graph is often misread. It is not zero resistance. It is extremely high resistance, so the current is negligible.

keyPoints.heading: Light-Dependent Resistors (LDRs)
keyPoints.content: An LDR (light-dependent resistor) is a component whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light, more photons hit the semiconductor material (often cadmium sulphide). This releases more charge carriers. So current flows more easily and resistance falls. In the dark, very few charge carriers are free. So resistance is very high, and can be hundreds of kΩ. In bright light, resistance can drop to just a few hundred ohms. Uses: - automatic street lights: dark → high resistance → the circuit switches the light on - burglar alarms: breaking a light beam changes the LDR's resistance, which sets off the alarm - camera exposure meters and garden solar lights An LDR can sit in a potential divider circuit with a fixed resistor. Its changing resistance shifts the voltage across each part. This voltage change can trigger a transistor switch. Graph shape: resistance on the y-axis, light intensity on the x-axis → a downward curve (not a straight line).
writeBullets: LDR — resistance decreases as light intensity increases
Dark — very high resistance (hundreds of kΩ). Bright light — low resistance (hundreds of Ω)
Semiconductor material releases more charge carriers in brighter light
Used in automatic street lights, burglar alarms and camera exposure meters
Paired with a fixed resistor in a potential divider. This gives a voltage signal that responds to light
Graph: resistance vs light intensity is a downward curve (inverse relationship)

keyTerms.def: Light-dependent resistor — a semiconductor component whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
A free electron or hole that can carry electric charge through a semiconductor material.
A circuit with two resistors in series; the output voltage depends on the ratio of the resistances.

keyPoints.memTip: More light → more carriers → more current → less resistance. Think of a crowd and doors. More light opens more doors, so it is easier to get through.
keyPoints.tutor_note: LDRs and thermistors are easy to mix up. Both are inverse: more means less resistance. But the trigger is different. An LDR responds to light. A thermistor responds to temperature.

keyPoints.heading: Thermistors
keyPoints.content: A thermistor is a component whose resistance decreases as temperature increases. The most common type is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient). The hotter it gets, the lower its resistance. At high temperatures, more electrons have enough thermal energy to break free from atoms. They act as charge carriers, so resistance falls a lot. At low temperatures, few carriers are free, so resistance is high. Worked example: at 20°C a thermistor might have R = 5000 Ω. At 100°C it might fall to 200 Ω. Uses: thermostats (central heating) and fire alarms. Also temperature sensors in car engines and medical devices, and smart home temperature controls. Key rule: the LDR and the thermistor are inverse components. More of the physical quantity (light or heat) → less resistance. A thermistor can sit in a potential divider. When the temperature crosses a set point, its change in resistance can trigger a switching circuit.
writeBullets: Thermistor — resistance decreases as temperature increases (NTC type)
More heat → more thermal energy → more free charge carriers → lower resistance
At low temperatures: high resistance. At high temperatures: low resistance
Used in thermostats, fire alarms and engine temperature sensors
Both LDR and thermistor: more of the physical quantity → less resistance
Graph: resistance vs temperature is a downward curve (not a straight line)

keyTerms.def: A temperature-sensitive resistor whose resistance decreases as temperature increases (NTC type).
Negative temperature coefficient — resistance decreases as temperature rises.
Energy associated with the temperature of a material; at higher temperatures, more electrons gain enough energy to become free charge carriers.

keyPoints.memTip: NTC = 'Nothing To Conduct when cold'. Heat it up and it conducts more easily. Its resistance goes down.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Common exam question: describe and explain the shape of a thermistor's resistance-temperature graph. Say that resistance decreases AND explain why: there are more carriers at higher temperature.

0.question: A fixed resistor has V = 12 V and I = 0.4 A. What is its resistance?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 Ω. Always check your units. Volts and amps give ohms.
0.wrongFeedback: Use R = V ÷ I. Divide 12 V by 0.4 A to get 30 Ω. Don't multiply or add. Ohm's Law is a division here.

1.question: On an I-V graph for a diode, what does the flat line at negative voltages show?
options: The diode has very high resistance, and almost no current flows in reverse bias
The diode allows equal current in both directions
1.correctFeedback: Spot on. In reverse bias the diode has extremely high resistance. The flat line shows that almost no current flows, even as the voltage grows more negative.
1.wrongFeedback: The flat line does NOT mean zero resistance. It means very high resistance, so the tiny current that does flow is negligible. The diode is blocking current in the reverse direction.

2.question: An LDR is moved from a bright room into a dark cupboard. What happens to its resistance?
2.correctFeedback: Exactly right. In the dark, fewer charge carriers are free. So it is harder for current to flow, and resistance increases a lot.
2.wrongFeedback: Remember: an LDR is an inverse component. MORE light = LESS resistance. So less light (a dark cupboard) means HIGHER resistance.

3.question: Both LDRs and thermistors are described as 'inverse' components. What does this mean?
options: As the physical quantity (light or heat) increases, resistance decreases
They only work when connected in reverse
Their I-V graphs are mirror images of each other
3.correctFeedback: Perfect. 'Inverse' means the relationship is opposite. More light or more heat leads to less resistance in both components.
3.wrongFeedback: Think about the LDR: bright light → low resistance. And the thermistor: hot → low resistance. Both respond to more of something by giving less resistance. That is what 'inverse' means here.

commonMistakes: Saying that protons move during friction charging. Only electrons transfer. Protons are fixed in the nucleus.
Mixing up the gradient of an I-V graph with resistance. A steeper line means lower resistance (more current per volt), not higher.
Thinking a diode has zero resistance in reverse bias. It has very HIGH resistance. So the current is negligible rather than truly zero.
Mixing up the LDR and thermistor. An LDR responds to light. A thermistor responds to temperature. Both drop in resistance as their quantity increases.
Forgetting that an LED is a type of diode. So it only conducts in the forward direction. It will not light up if it is connected the wrong way round.
examTips: When describing an LDR or thermistor, always give both parts. Say what happens to resistance AND explain why in terms of charge carriers.
For I-V graph questions, describe the shape exactly. For example: 'straight line through the origin', 'curve that gets less steep', or 'flat then sudden steep rise'. Vague answers lose marks.
You may be asked to pick the right fuse or explain how a circuit behaves. Write down V = IR first and start from there. Most electricity questions link back to it.
revisionCardBullets: Fixed resistor: constant resistance. Its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin
Variable resistor (rheostat): resistance changed by hand. Used in dimmer switches
Ohm's Law: V = IR (volts = amps × ohms)
Diode: current in one direction only. Threshold voltage ~0.7 V for silicon
LED: a diode that gives out light. Used in screens, traffic lights and energy-efficient bulbs
I-V graph for a diode: flat for negative V, steep rise above the threshold
LDR: more light → more charge carriers → less resistance
Thermistor (NTC): more heat → more charge carriers → less resistance
Both LDR and thermistor: inverse relationship between physical quantity and resistance
LDR uses: automatic street lights, burglar alarms, camera meters
Thermistor uses: thermostats, fire alarms, engine and medical temperature sensors
Potential divider: pair an LDR or thermistor with a fixed resistor. This gives a voltage signal that responds to light or heat
